question: What is Jetpack Compose? How is it different from the View system?
answer:
Jetpack Compose replaces the View system with `@Composable` functions that describe the UI for a given state.

The runtime calls those functions, builds a UI tree from what they emit, and calls them again when the state they read changes — that re-run is recomposition.

Differences vs the View system:
• Declarative — the UI is a function of state, not an imperative tree of mutable Views you keep in sync by hand.
• Kotlin only — no XML layouts, no findViewById, no view binding.
• Composition over inheritance — small functions instead of subclassing View.
• Animation, theming and accessibility (semantics) are first-class APIs rather than bolt-ons.
• Two-way interop — `AndroidView` hosts a View inside Compose and `ComposeView` hosts Compose inside an XML layout, so migration can be screen by screen.
• Material 3 components plus the `Modifier` chain replace styles, themes and drawable XML.

The setup detail interviewers do ask about: depend on the `androidx.compose:compose-bom` platform once and leave the individual compose artifacts version-less, so the whole set stays mutually compatible. Since Kotlin 2.0 the Compose compiler ships with Kotlin itself and is turned on by the `org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose` Gradle plugin — the old `composeOptions { kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion = ... }` block and its Kotlin-to-compiler version table are gone.

question: What are Modifiers in Compose and how do they work?
answer:
A `Modifier` is an ordered chain of decorations applied to a composable: size, padding, background, border, click handling, semantics.

• Order matters, and it is the number one Modifier interview question. `.padding(16.dp).background(Red)` paints red around the padded box; `.background(Red).padding(16.dp)` paints red behind the content only and puts the padding outside it. `.clickable` before `.padding` makes the padding tappable; after it, it does not.
• Modifiers are immutable values, so pass them as parameters to make a composable reusable.
• Every reusable composable should take `modifier: Modifier = Modifier` as its first optional parameter and apply it FIRST in its own chain, so the caller's decorations sit on the outside.
• Hoisting a chain into a `val` or a `remember` lets Compose reuse it instead of rebuilding it on every recomposition.
• A modifier that only reads state in layout or draw (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { }`, `drawBehind { }`) skips recomposition entirely.

For a custom modifier, `Modifier.then(...)` is enough to concatenate existing ones. Anything that needs its own state or coordinates should be a `Modifier.Node` implementation exposed through a `ModifierNodeElement`. `Modifier.composed { ... }` is the older factory and is discouraged: it forces an allocation at composition time and defeats the reuse the Node API was built for.

question: What are the main layout containers in Compose?
answer:
Compose has three basic layouts — Column stacks children vertically, Row horizontally, Box on the Z axis — plus lazy variants for long content.

• `Column` / `Row` — measure and place every child, so use them for a bounded number of items.
• `Box` — children overlap; `contentAlignment` sets the default and `Modifier.align` overrides it per child.
• `LazyColumn` / `LazyRow` — compose only the visible children. Mandatory for long or unbounded lists, and always pass a stable `key` in `items(...)`.
• `LazyVerticalGrid` / `LazyHorizontalGrid` with `GridCells.Fixed(n)` or `GridCells.Adaptive(minSize)`, plus `LazyVerticalStaggeredGrid` for uneven heights.
• `FlowRow` / `FlowColumn` — wrap children onto the next line when they run out of width; the idiomatic chip group.
• `ConstraintLayout` from `compose-constraintlayout` — only when a layout is genuinely relational. Nesting Rows and Columns is cheap in Compose because each child is measured exactly once, so the deep-hierarchy fear from the View system does not carry over.

`Modifier.weight` splits the leftover space inside a Row or Column, `Arrangement.spacedBy` gives even gaps more cleanly than padding on every child, and `Spacer` inserts a fixed gap. When none of the containers fit, `Layout` and `SubcomposeLayout` let you measure and place children yourself.

One rule to state explicitly: never put a `LazyColumn` inside a scrollable `Column` of the same direction — the infinite height constraint crashes or forces every item to compose.

question: What is recomposition, and what decides whether Compose skips a composable?
answer:
Recomposition is Compose re-running the composable functions whose inputs changed, to bring the UI back in line with state.

The runtime records which composable read which state object, so a write only re-runs the readers rather than the whole tree.

Key behaviours:
• A composable may run any number of times, in any order, and on any thread. It must be fast and free of side effects.
• Compose SKIPS a composable when all of its parameters compare equal to the previous call. Since strong skipping mode became the default (the Compose compiler shipped with Kotlin 2.0.20 and later), unstable parameters no longer block skipping — they are compared by instance identity instead — and lambdas are remembered automatically.
• Side effects belong in `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect` or `SideEffect`, never in the function body.
• Read state as low in the tree as you can: a value read only inside a leaf recomposes only that leaf.
• Compose runs three phases — composition, layout, draw. Deferring a read into a lambda (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { }`, or taking `() -> String` instead of `String`) keeps a fast-changing value out of composition so only layout or draw re-runs.

The consequence of strong skipping is that `@Immutable` / `@Stable` annotations and immutable collections are now a refinement that makes comparisons cheap and correct, not a prerequisite for skipping at all.

question: How does theming and Material 3 work in Compose?
answer:
Material 3 theming in Compose is one composable — `MaterialTheme` — holding a color scheme, a typography set and shapes that every component reads through composition locals.

• `MaterialTheme(colorScheme, typography, shapes) { content }` is the root; components read `MaterialTheme.colorScheme`, `MaterialTheme.typography`, `MaterialTheme.shapes`.
• `lightColorScheme(...)` / `darkColorScheme(...)` build the schemes. Every role has a matching `onX` color for the content drawn on top of it — using them is what keeps contrast correct.
• `dynamicLightColorScheme(context)` / `dynamicDarkColorScheme(context)` derive the palette from the wallpaper on Android 12 and later; guard the call by SDK level and keep a static fallback.
• `Surface` applies the background and the matching content color, and `LocalContentColor` carries that down the tree.
• Custom tokens (spacing, elevation, brand colors) belong in your own `CompositionLocal` beside MaterialTheme rather than crammed into it.

Dark mode comes from `isSystemInDarkTheme()` choosing the scheme, with an in-app setting able to override it.

Worth naming for currency: the Material 3 Expressive APIs — `MaterialExpressiveTheme`, a motion scheme and a wider shape scale — ship in the same `material3` artifact behind an experimental opt-in. They are additive and opt-in, so an existing `MaterialTheme` does not change under you.

question: How do you set up navigation in an Android app built with Jetpack Compose?
answer:
Navigation Compose gives an Android app one `NavHost` that owns a back stack of composable destinations, driven by a `NavController`.

The pieces:
• `rememberNavController()` creates the controller that owns the back stack.
• `NavHost(navController, startDestination)` declares the graph.
• `composable<Route> { ... }` registers a destination.
• `navController.navigate(route)` pushes and `popBackStack()` pops; `navigate(route) { popUpTo(Home) { inclusive = true }; launchSingleTop = true }` controls what the stack looks like afterwards.
• Each destination is its own `ViewModelStoreOwner` and `SavedStateRegistryOwner`, so a `viewModel()` or `hiltViewModel()` obtained inside a destination is scoped to that back-stack entry and dies with it. This Android-specific behaviour is the part interviewers actually probe.

Type-safe routes are the current default: mark a route as a `@Serializable` data class or data object and use `composable<Profile>` with `backStackEntry.toRoute<Profile>()`, instead of `"profile/{id}"` strings and `navArgument`. String routes still compile, and they are what you will find in code written before that API landed.

Two follow-ups to be ready for: deep links, declared with `navDeepLink<Profile>(basePath = ...)` on the destination and matched by an intent filter in the manifest; and returning a result to the previous screen, which goes through `previousBackStackEntry.savedStateHandle` rather than a shared singleton.

Alternatives exist — Voyager, Decompose, Compose Destinations — and Google is building Navigation 3, where the app owns the back stack as an ordinary list of keys. Check its stability before adopting it; Navigation Compose is still the safe answer for an Android app today.
